content: Cefaclor is indicated for the treatment of lower respiratory tract infections, including pneumonia, caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Streptococcus pyogenes. The recommended dosage for capsules is 250–500 mg orally every 8 hours. For otitis media caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, staphylococci, and Streptococcus pyogenes, the dosage is also 250–500 mg orally every 8 hours. Skin and skin structure infections caused by Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes are treated with 250–500 mg orally every 8 hours. Alternatively, extended-release tablets of 375 mg can be administered orally every 12 hours for 7–10 days. Urinary tract infections, including pyelonephritis and cystitis, caused by Escherichia coli, Proteus mirabilis, Klebsiella spp., and coagulase-negative staphylococci, are treated with 250–500 mg orally every 8 hours. Acute bacterial exacerbations of chronic bronchitis or secondary bacterial infections of acute bronchitis due to Haemophilus influenzae (excluding beta-lactamase-negative, ampicillin-resistant strains), Moraxella catarrhalis, or Streptococcus pneumoniae are treated with extended-release tablets of 500 mg orally every 12 hours for 7 days. Pharyngitis and tonsillitis caused by Streptococcus pyogenes are treated with 250–500 mg orally every 8 hours. Alternatively, extended-release tablets of 750 mg can be administered orally every 12 hours for 10 days. For patients with renal or hepatic impairment, no specific dosage adjustments are provided. However, beta-lactamase-negative, ampicillin-resistant (BLNAR) strains of Haemophilus influenzae should be considered resistant to cefaclor, even if in vitro susceptibility is observed in some strains. When treating beta-hemolytic streptococcal infections, the duration of therapy should be at least 10 days to ensure eradication of the pathogen. Cefaclor may interact with live bacterial vaccines, such as the BCG vaccine or cholera vaccine, by reducing their efficacy through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Administration of live bacterial vaccines should be delayed until the completion of antibiotic therapy. Similarly, oral or parenteral antibiotics administered within 14 days prior to vaccination may reduce the efficacy of the cholera vaccine. Cefaclor can decrease the effects of oral microbiota supplements containing bacterial spores due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Antibiotic regimens should be completed 2–4 days before initiating oral microbiota therapy. Cefaclor may increase the nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity of aminoglycosides such as amikacin, gentamicin, kanamycin, neomycin, streptomycin, and tobramycin. Caution and close monitoring are advised when co-administering these agents, as cephalosporins can enhance the nephrotoxic effects of aminoglycosides. Cefaclor may interfere with the therapeutic effects of immune checkpoint inhibitors, including atezolizumab, avelumab, balstilimab, camrelizumab, cemiplimab, cosibelimab, dostarlimab, durvalumab, nivolumab, pembrolizumab, penpulimab, retifanlimab, sintilimab, tislelizumab, and toripalimab. Caution and monitoring are recommended during co-administration. Cefaclor may reduce the efficacy of hormonal contraceptives, such as dienogest/estradiol valerate, estradiol, ethinyl estradiol, levonorgestrel/ethinyl estradiol/ferrous bisglycinate, and mestranol, by altering intestinal flora. While the risk of contraceptive failure is low, additional or alternative forms of birth control may be advisable during concomitant use. Cefaclor may increase the effects of acidic (anionic) drugs, such as probenecid, bendroflumethiazide, choline magnesium trisalicylate, piroxicam, salicylates (non-ASA), sulfasalazine, and willow bark, by competing for renal tubular clearance. The clinical significance of these interactions is generally minor or unknown, but monitoring is recommended. Cefaclor may increase the effects of warfarin, potentially enhancing anticoagulant activity. Caution and monitoring are advised during co-administration. Cefaclor may increase the toxicity of furosemide through pharmacodynamic synergism, leading to an increased risk of nephrotoxicity. Monitoring is recommended. Cefaclor levels may be increased by pretomanid and vadadustat due to inhibition of organic anion transporter 3 (OAT3). Close monitoring for adverse effects and potential dosage adjustments of OAT3 substrates are recommended. Cefaclor may decrease the effects of sodium picosulfate/magnesium oxide/anhydrous citric acid by altering colonic bacterial flora required for drug activation. Monitoring is advised during co-administration. Rose hips may increase cefaclor levels by competing for renal tubular clearance. The clinical significance of this interaction is minor or unknown. In summary, cefaclor has numerous pharmacological interactions that require careful consideration, monitoring, and, in some cases, alternative therapeutic strategies to ensure patient safety and treatment efficacy.
